chunks: "The core idea is that noise gets onto both wires at the same time and by about the same amount, and the receiver only looks at the difference.
So the noise is common-mode and it cancels, while the signal is opposite on the two wires, so it adds. Why is the noise the same on both wires?
Because the two wires are routed or twisted together.
A neighbouring trace couples capacitively into both, a magnetic field induces about the same voltage in both loops, and a ground shift moves both wires together.
In the receiver, the difference amplifier has a high common-mode rejection ratio, say 60 decibels, so half a volt of common-mode noise leaves about half a millivolt.
There are some extra bonuses. The signal is twice as big, so you get 6 decibels better signal-to-noise for the same swing per wire.
The threshold is the crossing point of the two wires, so it doesn't depend on a ground or supply reference that's moving around.
The equal and opposite currents mean it doesn't disturb its own ground or radiate much. The caveat is that the immunity is only as good as the symmetry.
If one wire sees more coupling, or the legs have skew, part of the common-mode noise turns into differential. A 1 percent imbalance limits the rejection to about 40 decibels."
